newsitem.title: UK: UK oil revenues dip on high pound, less output - bank.
newsitem.headline: UK oil revenues dip on high pound, less output - bank.

text.p: A strong pound and lower production and prices pushed British oil and gas revenues to their lowest for almost two years in June, the Royal Bank of Scotland said on Thursday
The decline in oil production was the seventh successive monthly fall but the bank's energy economist Stephen Boyle said the slide would not be permnanent.
"The falls are a product of seasonal maintenance and delays in commissioning some fields as others reach the end of their lives," he said in a statement issued by the bank.
Combined oil and gas revenue in June was down 12.6 percent from May to a provisional 34.9 million stg.
This is the lowest since August 1995 and well below a recent high of 60.1 million stg in January this year.
Oil production fell 12 percent to 2.15 million barrels per day (bpd) from 2.28 million bpd in May and 2.44 million bpd in June 1996.
The bank noted average daily production in the 12 months to June 1997 was 2.52 million bpd, only one percent lower than the previous 12 months.
"Price are likely to remain at around recent levels in the short run," Boyle added.
"If prices move out of their current range they are most likely to fall. Although demand is buoyant, supply is also growing strongly and stocks are strong."

The average price of Brent crude slid 8.1 percent to $17.70 and was four percent lower on an annual basis. The pound's strength meant the sterling price of Brent fell 8.7 percent in the month and 10 percent on the year.
Gas production fell 9.6 percent during June but was nevertheless 30.2 higher than in June 1996 thanks to 11 fields brought onstream in the past 12 months.

Some of the larger falls in oil production came from the following fields -- British Petroleum's Miller field (down 42,900 bpd), Mobil's Beryl field (down 13,619 bpd) and Amoco's Arbroath field (down 13,429 bpd).
Increases in production came from Shell's Gannet field (up 35,000 bpd), BP's Harding field (up 30,500 bpd) and Marathon's East Brae (up 9,000 bpd).
Britain's North Sea oil and gas industry contributed 3.6 billion stg in tax revenue to government coffers in the fiscal year 1996/97, up from 2.35 billion stg the year before.
